newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin rejects draft law on keeping WW2 art booty.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin rejects draft law on keeping WW2 art booty.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin on Tuesday vetoed a draft law claiming ownership of art booty seized from Nazi Germany and its allies during World War Two, the presidential press service said.

The draft document, which would turn all valuable works of art brought to the Soviet Union during the war into Russian property, was approved by both houses of parliament and only needed Yeltsin's signature to become law.
But Yeltsin wrote to the head of the Federation Council upper house, Yegor Stroyev, saying he rejected the law because he believed it contradicted international law.

"The (draft) federal law makes the priority a one-sided decision on claiming art treasures without taking into account the norms of international legislation and results of negotiations," Yeltsin wrote in the letter.
He also said the document could damage Russia's position in talks with Germany, France, Poland, Hungary, the Netherlands and Liechtenstein -- countries from which the works of art came.
Parliament could return the draft law to Yeltsin again, but it would need to muster the support of two-thirds of a joint assembly of the two chambers.
The draft law has been criticised by both Russian and German governments.

Germany has demanded the return of the artefacts, which include priceless painting by French impressionists Monet and Matisse, as well as the Schliemann collection of golden treasures from ancient Troy, and appealed several times to Yeltsin for help.

Yeltsin also criticised the law, saying it did not distinguish between Moscow's wartime enemies, allies and neutral countries, or between various categories of private individuals with rights to claim objects back.
"At the same time, the federal property status on all artefacts may cause legal problems with arranging exhibitions abroad and the very impossibility of exhibiting them," the letter said.
German sources earlier said they expected Yeltsin would block the law. A joint German-Russian government commission was looking for a way to resolve the situation calmly, they said.
Many Russians view the seized treasures as compensation for wartime suffering in the Soviet Union and for the many Russian treasures the Nazis destroyed.
